::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

A choropleth shades geographic units by value, but the human eye reads ink by **area**, not by population or intensity. Mapping raw totals mostly redraws population or country size, small denominators produce the wildest extreme rates, and switching between equal-interval, quantile, and natural-breaks classes changes which regions look alarming. Before publishing any shaded map, normalize to a rate or density, check small-denominator noise, and state the unit, denominator, and classification scheme in the caption.
:::

## 1. Ink follows area, not people

On a world or county map, a large rural unit takes up far more pixels than a dense city or small nation. Even when both carry the same color, the large polygon dominates visual attention.

- **Fix:** When geographic area is not the denominator of interest, pair the choropleth with a cartogram (scaling area by population) or a dot-density / proportional-symbol layer so visual weight matches the quantity being compared.

## 2. Counts versus rates

Consider mapping national fertilizer use in tonnes (`Fert.tonnes` from FAO-style country tables joined to `rworldmap::getMap()`). Plotting raw tonnes highlights large agricultural producers (China, India, the United States) simply because they have more farmland—not necessarily because application intensity is highest.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Raw Counts<br/>Total tonnes] --> B{Normalize by<br/>area or population?}
    B -- No --> C[Redraws country size<br/>or population]
    B -- Yes --> D[Rate / Intensity<br/>kg per hectare or per capita]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## View R code: joining country totals to `rworldmap` polygons

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(rworldmap)
library(RColorBrewer)

# sample_data.csv is not included: one row per country and year, with columns
# Entity, Year and a fourth column holding total fertilizer use in tonnes.
raw_data <- read.csv("sample_data.csv")
colnames(raw_data)[4] <- "Fert.tonnes"

world_map <- ggplot2::fortify(rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low"))
map_1996 <- world_map %>%
  dplyr::left_join(raw_data, by = c("id" = "Entity")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(Year == 1996)

ggplot(map_1996, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = Fert.tonnes), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colors = rev(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(11, "Spectral")),
    guide = guide_colorbar(title = "tonnes", nbin = 15, raster = FALSE)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```
:::

- **Fix:** Divide counts by cropland area (`kg/ha`) or population (`kg/person`) before shading, and state the denominator explicitly in the legend title.

## 3. Small numbers make loud rates

Once you convert counts to rates ($\text{rate}_i = y_i / n_i$), variance scales inversely with the denominator $n_i$:

$$\text{Var}(\hat{p}_i) \approx \frac{p(1 - p)}{n_i}$$

A small island nation or low-population county with $n_i = 20$ fluctuates wildly by chance, so the highest and lowest rates on a map almost always belong to the smallest units.

- **Fix:** Show the underlying count alongside the rate in tooltips or labels, apply empirical Bayes smoothing for noisy small-area rates, or mask units below a minimum sample threshold.

## 4. Binning writes the story

The same numeric vector produces completely different maps depending on how continuous values are binned into color classes:

| Classification Scheme | How Breakpoints Are Chosen | Visual Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Equal interval** (`equal`) | Divides $[\min, \max]$ into $k$ equal-width steps | Highlights extreme outliers; most units collapse into the bottom bin |
| **Quantile** (`quantile`) | Places an equal number of units in each bin | Maximizes contrast across the map, but can group very different values together |
| **Natural breaks** (`fisher`) | Minimizes within-class variance | Preserves data clusters, but breakpoints are dataset-specific and hard to compare across years |

- **Fix:** Choose the scheme that matches your question (use consistent breakpoints across time-series panels) and name the scheme in the figure caption.

## What this means for you

Before putting any county, state, or country choropleth into a report:

1. Check whether raw totals are just acting as a proxy for area or population.
2. Verify that extreme rates aren't artifacts of tiny denominators.
3. State the **geographic unit**, **denominator**, and **classification scheme** in the caption.

## Key takeaways

- A choropleth of raw counts is close to a population or area map for most human and agricultural variables.
- Equal-interval, quantile, and Fisher-Jenks binning (`classInt::classIntervals(style = ...)`) on the exact same data can assign the same region to opposite ends of the color scale.
- In a rate map, the smallest units have the highest sampling variance and are the most likely to show extreme rates.
- Changing aggregation boundaries changes the apparent spatial pattern (the **modifiable areal unit problem**).
